Contemporary Worship Music
kun-TEM-puh-rair-ee WUR-ship MYOO-zik
noun phrase (ecclesiastical, descriptive)
From Latin contemporaneus, of the same time; modern song forms used in the gathered worship of the church.

Biblical Definition

Contemporary worship music names the modern song forms increasingly used in church gatherings, and it must be measured—like all worship—by the regulative principle and the priority of the Word, not by mere antiquity or novelty. Scripture commands that the saints sing, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with grace in the heart unto the Lord; and that all things be done decently and in order. The age of a tune is not the test. A song penned this year may be saturated with truth, and an ancient one may be empty. The genuine question is whether the singing serves the Word—teaching sound doctrine, exalting God, and edifying the body—or whether it has become an end in itself. Here lies the live temptation. Modern worship readily drifts toward pragmatism, choosing songs because they fill seats; toward entertainment, treating the gathering as performance with the congregation as audience and the platform as stage; and toward emotionalism, manufacturing feeling by volume, repetition, and atmosphere rather than feeding affection from truth. These are real dangers to name plainly. Yet they are not arguments against all modern composition, for the church in every age has written new songs to the Lord, and the Psalter itself bids us sing a new song. The Reformed conscience does not bind the church to a single century's music; it binds her to sing truth, in order, for edification, with reverence, that the Word of Christ may dwell richly and God alone be magnified.

Webster 1828 Definition

Contemporary worship music is modern song used in church, to be weighed by the regulative principle and the priority of the Word.

CONTEMPORARY WORSHIP MUSIC, noun phrase. From Latin contemporaneus, of the same time.

Modern song forms employed in the gathered worship of the church.

Music subject, like all elements of worship, to the rule of Scripture and the priority of the Word.

Prone to particular temptations: pragmatism, entertainment, and manufactured emotion.

Scripture commands the substance: "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly... teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs" (Colossians 3:16).

Key Scripture

Col 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."

Eph 5:19 — "Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord."

1Co 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

Psa 96:1 — "O sing unto the LORD a new song: sing unto the LORD, all the earth."

Modern Corruption

The temptation is to bend worship toward entertainment, pragmatism, and emotion rather than the Word.

expand to see more

The modernist drift recasts the gathering as a "worship experience"—a produced event judged by how it makes the crowd feel, with darkened rooms, swelling sound, and endless repetition engineered to manufacture sentiment. Songs are chosen to draw and retain a crowd rather than to teach the truth; the congregation becomes an audience watching a platform; and feeling is pumped up by atmosphere instead of being kindled by the knowledge of God. This is the pragmatism, entertainment, and emotionalism that the Reformed conscience must name plainly. It empties singing of its appointed work, which is to let the Word of Christ dwell richly through doctrine sung.

The recovery is neither a blanket condemnation of modern composition nor an uncritical embrace of it. The Psalter itself commands a new song, and faithful believers in our day have written hymns rich with truth. The measure is fixed: does the singing teach sound doctrine, exalt God, and edify the body, done decently and in order under the priority of the Word? Where modern songs meet that test they may be sung with joy; where they trade truth for spectacle they must be refused. The church is bound not to a century but to the rule of Scripture.

Hebrew Roots

The doctrine rests on the biblical commands to sing the Word with order and reverence.

expand to see more

Colossians 3:16 ties singing to the rich indwelling of the Word and to mutual teaching.

Ephesians 5:19 commands psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs made to the Lord from the heart.

1 Corinthians 14:40 requires all worship to be done decently and in order.

Psalm 96:1 commands the singing of a new song, sanctioning fresh composition under truth.

The regulative principle measures every element of worship by the warrant of Scripture.

Usage

"Used descriptively of modern song styles: "the church introduced contemporary worship music.""

"Used in critique: "contemporary worship music can drift toward entertainment.""

"Used in commendation: "some contemporary worship music is rich in doctrine.""
